overview: This file contains a State Department cross-reference sheet and a duplicate of despatch No. 323 from John Cudahy in Warsaw concerning reports of a “Central Japanese News Bureau for Europe.” Cudahy reports that no such bureau could be found in Warsaw or elsewhere in Poland and suggests that observers may have mistaken the small RIENT agency—an anti-Soviet, pro-Japanese operation run by Caucasian émigré Vassan-Girey Dzhabagiev with several Russian associates—for an official Japanese organization. The despatch also records that the Japanese military attaché’s office in Warsaw served as an evaluation center for intelligence collected in Poland and the Baltic states.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 323 on the alleged Japanese news bureau in Warsaw
subfiles.about: Cudahy reports the results of an investigation into an alleged Central Japanese News Bureau for Europe and describes the possibly confused RIENT agency.
subfiles.summary: A careful embassy investigation found no Central Japanese News Bureau for Europe or comparable organization in Warsaw or elsewhere in Poland. Cudahy suggests that an observer may have mistaken RIENT—an obscure agency closely at home in the Japanese Legation and operated by Vassan-Girey Dzhabagiev with Russian émigré associates—for a Japanese bureau. RIENT distributed anti-Soviet and pro-Japanese news and articles to a small clientele from Dzhabagiev’s apartment. Cudahy adds that the Japanese military attaché’s office in Warsaw evaluated information gathered by Japanese military attachés in Poland and the Baltic states.

interest: The file is useful for studying the blurred boundary between news gathering, propaganda, émigré politics, and military intelligence in interwar Eastern Europe. Its description of the obscure RIENT agency supplies rare details about its personnel, political orientation, limited operations, and apparent familiarity with the Japanese Legation. The passing observation about Warsaw’s role in Japan’s military-attaché intelligence network is especially significant, while the cross-reference sheet illustrates how related evidence could be dispersed across different State Department decimal-file classifications.
